plate_findings.evidence: (A) a solitary violaceous plaque with hyperkeratotic surface on limbs

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Caption explicitly attributes solitary violaceous hyperkeratotic plaque to M. marinum infection; image shows hyperkeratotic violaceous plaque on knee matching verrucous granulomatous morphology. B: Caption attributes multiple violaceous hyperkeratotic plaques to M. marinum; image shows multiple plaques on leg. C: Caption directly describes warty verrucous plaque on hand due to M. marinum; image shows violaceous verrucous plaque on dorsal hand/finger web. D: Caption attributes (D) erythematous swelling of finger with pus discharge to M. marinum infection and in-text describes ulcerative wounds with purulent discharge; image shows inflamed swollen finger with discharge. No vocabulary finding_key covers purulent ulcerative swelling, so captured in proposed_findings.
panels.attribution_text: Wu et al. Fish tank granuloma caused by Mycobacterium marinum.. PloS one 2012. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0041296. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Cutaneous manifestations of Mycobacterium marinum infections. Footnote: M. marinum skin infections presented with (A) a solitary, or (B) multiple violaceous plaques with hyperkeratotic surface on limbs. The disease also presented as (C) a warty, verrucous plaque with an irregular border on hand, or (D) erythematous swelling of finger with pus discharge.
in_text_mentions: These patients did not consult a doctor until the symptoms worsened; the duration from the onset of symptoms to visiting a doctor varied from 15 days to as long as 3 years. The most common presentations were tender, erythematous nodules or plaques (18/27). Seven of the 27 patients presented with ulcerative wounds with a purulent discharge (figure 1). One of these patients had corneal involvement and complained of right-eye pain and photophobia, and another patient had dyspnea.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photo of left upper limb with linear ascending ulcerated nodular granulomatous lesions in article titled Mycobacterium marinum Infection Leading to HIV Diagnosis; matches sporotrichoid lymphangitic spread, classic for fish-tank granuloma.
panels.attribution_text: Yasuda et al. Mycobacterium marinum Infection Leading to HIV Diagnosis: A Case Report.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.73016. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Clinical presentation A well-demarcated skin ulcer surrounded by erythematous tissue, with multiple nodular and granulomatous lesions, extending from the patient's left hand to the forearm.
in_text_mentions: A 54-year-old male noticed a gradually enlarging skin ulcer on his left upper limb. Initially, he visited a local clinic where sporotrichosis was suspected based on the linear pattern of the ulcer, and he was prescribed oral itraconazole for one month. However, the condition did not improve; therefore, he was referred to our hospital to evaluate his skin eruption. Upon examination, he presented with a well-demarcated skin ulcer surrounded by erythematous tissue with multiple roundish ulcers resembling a nodular granulomatous pattern (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: Histological examination of the lesion shows a hyperplastic epidermis and a dense cell infiltrate in the dermis

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is H&E histology of skin biopsy from M. marinum case showing hyperplastic epidermis and dense dermal infiltrate consistent with suppurative granulomatous inflammation; article title is disease-focused and caption attributes lesion to the infection. B: Panel B is higher magnification histology showing polymorphous infiltrate with macrophages, neutrophils and multinucleated giant cells surrounding pre-necrotic foci, matching suppurative granuloma of M. marinum infection. C: Panel C is higher magnification histology showing same polymorphous granulomatous infiltrate with giant cells and pre-necrotic areas, matching suppurative granuloma of M. marinum infection.
panels.attribution_text: Assiri et al. Cutaneous Mycobacterium Marinum Infection (Fish Tank Granuloma) in a Renal Transplant Recipient: Case Report and Literature Review.. Cureus 2019. doi:10.7759/cureus.6013. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Microscopic examination of the skin biopsy A) Histological examination of the lesion shows a hyperplastic epidermis and a dense cell infiltrate in the dermis; B-C) On higher magnification, the infiltrate consists of lymphocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, and multinucleated giant cells. The dermis contains granular, basophilic, pre-necrotic areas.
in_text_mentions: Microscopic examination of the skin biopsy showed a hyperplastic epidermis and a dense polymorphous dermal infiltrate made of lymphocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, and multinucleated giant cells, occasionally surrounding pre-necrotic foci in the mid-dermis (Figure 2A-C).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photo of a 3-year-old girl's hand dorsum showing an erythematous lump over the third and fourth digits; caption and article title attribute this to Mycobacterium marinum infection after an iguana bite. Real human-patient image of a specific cutaneous manifestation. B: Ultrasound of the same patient's hand mass with numbered digit labels; it images the M. marinum lesion (though the sonographic appearance was nonspecific and initially suggestive of a ganglion cyst). Real patient image, so included with a proposed finding rather than a vocabulary key. C: H&E histology from the patient's hand mass showing necrotizing/suppurative granulomatous inflammation, a specific histopathologic manifestation of M. marinum infection. D: Fite-stained histology from the same patient showing numerous acid-fast mycobacteria within necrosis, a specific microbiologic/histopathologic manifestation of M. marinum infection.

panels.figure_caption: Gross and microscopic features of a mass involving the dorsum of the left hand in a 3-year-old girl with Mycobacterium marinum infection after iguana bite in Costa Rica. A) Erythematous lump over third and fourth digits. B) Ultrasound image, with numbers labeling the digits. C) Hematoxylin and eosin–stained soft tissue showing granulomatous inflammation. Scale bar indicates 10 µm. D) Fite stain highlighting numerous mycobacteria in an area of necrosis. Scale bar indicates 20 µm.
in_text_mentions: small lump on the dorsum of her left hand that was not present previously. The child was otherwise well. The lump became progressively larger, erythematous, and mildly painful over the next 3 months (Figure, panel A). Because of persistent symptoms, her parents sought medical attention at Stanford Medicine Children’s Health (Stanford, California, USA). Although ultrasound demonstrated findings suggestive of a ganglion cyst (Figure, panel B), the location and symptoms were not consistent with this diagnosis. She saw an orthopedic surgeon who, given the progression and unusual clinical features,

third and fourth digits, with extrusion of a thick, white, purulent material. Histopathology revealed extensive necrosis and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli seen by Fite staining (Figure, panels C, D). Bacterial 16S rRNA sequencing identified a sequence with 100% identity to M. marinum (GenBank accession no. OQ249694). Mycobacterial culture (Middlebrook 7H11 agar) incubated at 30°C grew photochromogenic colonies after 2 weeks that were consistent with M. marinum. The patient was started on rifampin and clarithromycin and gradually improved over the next 2 months.
